problem: 'paysannes and Bäuerinnen' (French and German for peasant women) is unexplained; a listener will not catch it. Add a brief gloss.
new_text: Mr. Rivers came up just as I had watched the classes — now numbering sixty girls — file out before me and had locked the door. I stood with the key in my hand, exchanging a few words of special farewell with some half-dozen of my best pupils: as decent, respectable, modest, and well-informed young women as could be found in the ranks of the British peasantry. And that is saying a great deal; for after all, the British peasantry are the best taught, best mannered, and most self-respecting of any in Europe: since those days I have seen French and German peasant girls — paysannes and Bäuerinnen — and the best of them seemed to me ignorant, coarse, and besotted compared with my Morton girls.

problem: Reported (indirect) speech is placed inside quotation marks with a question mark (he asked, "If I was at last satisfied...?"), which reads/sounds garbled to a modern reader. Render as plain indirect speech.
new_text: St. John arrived first. I had begged him to keep quite clear of the house till everything was arranged, and indeed the bare idea of the commotion — at once sordid and trivial — going on within its walls was enough to drive him to stay away. He found me in the kitchen, watching the progress of certain cakes for tea, then baking. Approaching the hearth, he asked if I was at last satisfied with housemaid’s work. I answered by inviting him to accompany me on a general inspection of the result of my labours. With some difficulty, I got him to make the tour of the house. He just looked in at the doors I opened; and when he had wandered upstairs and downstairs, he said I must have gone through a great deal of fatigue and trouble to have effected such considerable changes in so short a time — but not a syllable did he utter to indicate pleasure in the improved appearance of his home.

problem: The whole paragraph is St. John's reply in third-person indirect speech but wrapped in quotation marks ('he had... noticed that I had...'), so a listener hears a quoted speech in which 'he' and 'I' seem to refer to the wrong people. Remove the quote marks and attribute it.
new_text: Not at all, he said; on the contrary, he had noticed that I had scrupulously respected every association: he feared, indeed, I must have bestowed more thought on the matter than it was worth. How many minutes, for instance, had I devoted to studying the arrangement of this very room? By the way, could I tell him where such a book was?

problem: 'Caffre bush' is an obsolete (and now offensive) term a modern reader will not understand; the geographic sense is 'the South African bush'.
new_text: “This parlour is not his sphere,” I reflected. “The Himalayan ridge or South African bush, even the plague-cursed Guinea Coast swamp would suit him better. Well may he shun the calm of domestic life; it is not his element — there his faculties stagnate, they cannot develop or appear to advantage. It is in scenes of strife and danger — where courage is proved, and energy exercised, and fortitude tested — that he will speak and move, the leader and superior. A merry child would have the advantage of him on this hearth. He is right to choose a missionary’s career — I see it now.”

problem: Missing article: 'He gave each one quiet kiss'.
new_text: They were stiff from their long and jolting drive from Whitcross, and chilled from the frosty night air; but their pleasant faces brightened in the cheerful firelight. While the driver and Hannah brought in the boxes, they asked for St. John. At that moment he came out from the parlour. They both threw their arms round his neck at once. He gave each one a quiet kiss, said in a low tone a few words of welcome, stood a while to be talked to, and then, hinting that he supposed they would soon rejoin him in the parlour, withdrew there as to a place of refuge.

problem: Spelling of the language differs within the batch: 'Hindostanee' in ch. 34 vs 'Hindustani' in ch. 37. Use the modern spelling 'Hindustani' throughout.
new_text: “I want you to give up German and learn Hindustani.”

He then went on to explain that Hindustani was the language he was himself studying at present; that as he advanced, he was apt to forget the beginning; that it would help him greatly to have a pupil with whom he might go over the elements again and again, and so fix them thoroughly in his mind; that his choice had hovered for some time between me and his sisters; but that he had settled on me because he saw I could sit at a task the longest of the three. Would I do him this favour? I should not, perhaps, have to make the sacrifice long, as it now wanted barely three months to his departure.

A fine spring shone round me, which I could not enjoy. Summer approached; Diana tried to cheer me: she said I looked ill, and wished to accompany me to the seaside. This St. John opposed; he said I did not need dissipation, I needed employment; my present life was too purposeless, I needed an aim; and, I suppose, by way of supplying deficiencies, he prolonged still further my lessons in Hindustani, and grew more urgent in demanding their completion: and I, like a fool, never thought of resisting him — I could not resist him.

problem: 'coadjutor' is an obscure word for a modern reader/listener; 'co-worker' (or 'fellow worker') keeps the meaning.
new_text: “Well — well. To the main point — the departure with me from England, the co-operation with me in my future labours — you do not object. You have already as good as put your hand to the plough: you are too consistent to withdraw it. You have but one end to keep in view — how the work you have undertaken can best be done. Simplify your complicated interests, feelings, thoughts, wishes, aims; merge all considerations in one purpose: that of fulfilling with effect — with power — the mission of your great Master. To do so, you must have a co-worker: not a brother — that is a loose tie — but a husband. I, too, do not want a sister: a sister might any day be taken from me. I want a wife: the sole helpmeet I can influence effectively in life, and retain absolutely till death.”

problem: 'a neophyte's respect and submission to his hierophant' — both words are obscure; gloss plainly (a novice to his high priest).
new_text: “It would do,” I affirmed with some disdain, “perfectly well. I have a woman’s heart, but not where you are concerned; for you I have only a comrade’s constancy; a fellow-soldier’s frankness, fidelity, fraternity, if you like; a novice’s respect and submission to his high priest: nothing more — don’t fear.”

problem: Diana has just urged Jane to give up going; Jane's bare reply "I must" can be heard as 'I must go', the opposite of what the rest of her speech means (she has to give it up because St. John rejected her offer). Make it explicit.
new_text: "I must give it up," I said. "Just now, when I repeated my offer to serve as his assistant, he was appalled by my lack of propriety. He seemed to think I'd done something indecent in proposing to travel with him unmarried—as if I hadn't always hoped to find a brother in him and regarded him as one."

problem: 'as that phantom rose up dark beside the black yew tree' — 'that phantom' has no antecedent, so a reader may think a ghost actually appeared. It is the phantom of superstition itself.
new_text: "Down, superstition!" I told myself, as that phantom of superstition rose up dark beside the black yew tree at the gate. "This is not deception, nor witchcraft. It is the work of nature. She was stirred, and she performed—no miracle—but her finest work."

problem: "I mean the present gentleman, Mr. Edward's father" reads as if 'the present gentleman' is the father — the opposite of the intended meaning (the late Mr. Rochester is the father of the present gentleman, Mr. Edward). The next sentences depend on this being clear.
new_text: "I mean the present gentleman's father—old Mr. Rochester, Mr. Edward's father," he explained. I breathed again. My blood flowed once more. Those words fully assured me that Mr. Edward—my Mr. Rochester, God bless him wherever he was!—was at least alive. Was, in fact, "the present gentleman." What comforting words! It seemed I could now bear whatever came next—whatever the revelations might be—with relative calm. Since he was not in the grave, I could endure hearing he was at the other end of the earth.

problem: 'brownie' will be heard as the chocolate cake; the folklore sense (a shaggy household goblin) needs a brief gloss.
new_text: "Just to comb out this shaggy black mane. I find you rather alarming at close range. You talk of my being a fairy, but I'm sure you look more like a brownie—a shaggy little goblin—yourself."
